2009B16.goal: $BA$ and $BC$ are tangents from $B$ to a circle centred at $O$, and $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral. $D$ is where $BO$ meets the circle. We want $\tfrac{BD}{BO}$. Find $\angle OBA$.

tools.name: Tangent ⟂ radius
tools.why: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

tools.name: Tangents are symmetric
tools.why: The two tangent segments from $B$ are mirror images in $BO$.

tools.name: 30-60-90 triangle
tools.why: $\sin30^\circ=\tfrac12$.

2009B16.approach: $\angle ABO=30^\circ$, so in right triangle $OAB$ the hypotenuse $BO$ is twice the short leg $OA=r$. Then $BD=BO-r=r$.

steps.title: The angle
steps.explain: $\angle ABC=60^\circ$ and $BO$ bisects it: $\angle ABO=30^\circ$. Triangle $OAB$ has a right angle at $A$.

check.q: In right triangle $OAB$ with $\angle B=30^\circ$ and $OA=r$, what is $BO$?
check.why: $OA$ is opposite $30^\circ$, so it is half the hypotenuse.

steps.title: The ratio
steps.explain: $D$ lies between $B$ and $O$ at distance $r$ from $O$, so $BD=2r-r=r$ and $\tfrac{BD}{BO}=\tfrac12$.

2009B16.shortcut: Tangents at $60^\circ$ apart put $B$ at distance $2r$: $D$ is the midpoint of $BO$.
traps: Taking $D$ on the far side of $O$.
2009B16.recognize: Tangents from an external point: the line to the centre bisects the angle and makes right triangles with the radii.

2009B17.goal: Five unit squares (total area $5$) are cut by the line from $(c,0)$ to $(3,3)$ into equal halves. We want $c$. The part of the region below the line is the right triangle $(c,0),(3,0),(3,3)$ minus the one unit square inside that triangle that is not part of the region.

tools.name: Right-triangle area
tools.why: Legs along $y=0$ and $x=3$.

tools.name: Equal halves
tools.why: Total area $5$.

2009B17.approach: In the figure, the region's part on the lower-right side of the line is the triangle with vertices $(c,0),(3,0),(3,3)$ with exactly one empty unit square removed. Set that equal to $\tfrac52$.
2009B17.bridge: Triangle area minus the empty square equals half of $5$.
2009B17.shortcut: Use one big easy shape (the triangle) and subtract what isn't there, instead of adding pieces.
traps: Forgetting to subtract the empty square.
Setting the triangle equal to $5$ instead of $\tfrac52$.
2009B17.recognize: Area bisection by a line: write one side's area as a simple shape plus or minus whole squares.

2009B18.goal: Rectangle $AB=8$, $BC=6$; $M$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $E$ on $AB$ has $ME\perp AC$. We want $[AME]$. Triangle $AME$ has a right angle at $M$ and shares $\angle A$ with triangle $ABC$.

tools.name: Diagonal
tools.why: Pythagoras.

tools.name: Similar right triangles
tools.why: Both have a right angle and share $\angle A$.

2009B18.approach: $AM=5$. With $\tan A=\tfrac{BC}{AB}=\tfrac34$, the leg $ME=\tfrac34\cdot5$. Area is half the product of the legs.
2009B18.recognize: A perpendicular dropped onto a diagonal makes a triangle similar to the half-rectangle.

2009B19.goal: A 12-hour clock shows $9$ wherever it should show $1$. We want the fraction of the day it is right, i.e. the fraction of times whose display contains no digit $1$. Hours and minutes are independent.

tools.name: Independence
tools.why: Every hour pairs with every minute equally.

tools.name: Digit-by-digit
tools.why: Minutes $00$–$59$ use every tens/units combination.

2009B19.approach: Hours $1$–$12$: $1,10,11,12$ contain a $1$, leaving $8$ of $12$. Minutes: tens digit $0$–$5$ (avoid $1$: $\tfrac56$), units digit $0$–$9$ (avoid $1$: $\tfrac9{10}$).

check.q: How many of the hours $1$–$12$ contain the digit $1$?

2009B19.bridge: Multiply the hour fraction by the two minute-digit fractions.
traps: Treating the tens digit of minutes as $0$–$9$.
2009B19.recognize: "Avoid a digit" on clocks: split into independent digit positions with their own ranges.

2009B20.goal: Right triangle with legs $AB=1$, $BC=2$; the bisector of $\angle A$ meets $BC$ at $D$. We want $BD$. The angle bisector theorem splits $BC$ in the ratio of the adjacent sides.

tools.name: Angle bisector theorem
tools.why: The bisector from $A$ divides the opposite side in the ratio of the sides at $A$.

tools.name: Hypotenuse
tools.why: Pythagoras.

2009B20.bridge: Apply the bisector theorem, then rationalise.
2009B20.recognize: Angle bisector meeting the opposite side: use the ratio of the two adjacent sides.

2009B21.goal: We want $3^0+3^1+\cdots+3^{2009}\pmod 8$. Powers of $3$ mod $8$ alternate $1,3,1,3,\ldots$

tools.name: Cycle of powers
tools.why: So $3^{\text{even}}\equiv1$, $3^{\text{odd}}\equiv3$.

tools.name: Pairing
tools.why: Group consecutive terms.

2009B21.approach: There are $2010$ terms, i.e. $1005$ pairs, each $\equiv4$. The sum is $\equiv4\cdot1005\pmod8$.

steps.title: Pairs
steps.explain: Each pair $(3^{2k},3^{2k+1})$ is $\equiv1+3=4\pmod8$; there are $1005$ pairs.

2009B21.shortcut: Closed form: the sum is $\tfrac{3^{2010}-1}{2}$. Since $9^2\equiv1\pmod{16}$, $3^{2010}=9^{1005}\equiv9\pmod{16}$, and $\tfrac{9-1}{2}=4$.
traps: Concluding $0$ because each pair is divisible by $4$.
2009B21.recognize: Long sums of powers mod $m$: find the cycle of the powers and group by cycle.

2009B22.goal: A $2\times2\times2$ cake is iced on top and sides and cut vertically. In the top view (square side $2$, $M$ the midpoint of the top edge) one cut runs from $M$ to a bottom corner and the other from the other bottom corner perpendicular to the first cut. Piece $B$ has top triangle with the bottom edge as one side. We want volume $c$ plus icing $s$.

tools.name: Prism volume
tools.why: Vertical cuts make a prism of height $2$.

tools.name: Icing on a piece
tools.why: Only faces on the outside of the cube are iced; the bottom is not.

tools.name: Foot of a perpendicular
tools.why: Finds where the second cut meets the first.

2009B22.approach: Place the square at $(0,0)$–$(2,2)$ with $M=(1,2)$. The cut is from $(0,0)$ to $M$, direction $(1,2)$. The perpendicular from $(2,0)$ lands at $N=(\tfrac25,\tfrac45)$. Triangle $B$ has vertices $(0,0),(2,0),N$; height $\tfrac45$ over base $2$.

check.q: A triangle with base $2$ on the $x$-axis and third vertex at height $\tfrac45$ has area?

steps.title: Volume and icing
steps.explain: $c=\tfrac45\cdot2=\tfrac85$. Icing: top $\tfrac45$ plus the outer side face $2\times2=4$, so $s=\tfrac{24}5$. Sum $\tfrac{32}5$.

check.q: Which faces of piece $B$ are iced?
check.why: Cut faces are inside the cake; the bottom is not iced.

2009B22.bridge: Find the triangle's area; volume is twice it, icing is it plus the outer side.
2009B22.shortcut: $c+s=3\cdot(\text{top area})+2\cdot(\text{outer edge})$ for any vertical slice of this cake.
traps: Icing the cut faces or the bottom.
2009B22.recognize: Vertical slices of a prism: volume is area times height; surface counts only original outside faces.

2009B23.goal: Rachel laps in $90$ s, Robert (other direction) in $80$ s. A photo at a random time between $600$ and $660$ s shows the quarter of track centred on the start. We want the probability both are in it. Each runner is in the photo when within $\tfrac18$ lap of the start.

tools.name: Windows around lap times
tools.why: $\tfrac18$ lap takes $\tfrac T8$ seconds; direction doesn't matter.

tools.name: Uniform time
tools.why: The photo time is uniform on $[600,660]$.

2009B23.approach: Rachel passes the start at $630$ (lap $7$); she is in view for $630\pm11.25$. Robert passes at $640$ (lap $8$); in view for $640\pm10$. Intersect with each other and $[600,660]$.

steps.title: Windows
steps.explain: Rachel: $[618.75,641.25]$. Robert: $[630,650]$. (Their other passes, $540,720$ and $560,720$, are too far.)

check.q: How long does Rachel take to run $\tfrac18$ lap?

2009B23.bridge: Find each runner's in-view interval during minute $10$ and intersect.
solution: Rachel is at the start at $t=630$, in view on $[618.75,641.25]$.
Robert is at the start at $t=640$, in view on $[630,650]$.
2009B23.shortcut: Directions are irrelevant: only distance from the start matters.
traps: Using a window of $\tfrac14$ lap on each side.
2009B23.recognize: Periodic motion + random observation time: turn each condition into time intervals and measure the overlap.

2009B24.goal: An arch of $9$ congruent isosceles trapezoids, end bottoms horizontal. We want the larger interior angle $x$. Extend each trapezoid's legs: they meet at the arch's centre, and the $9$ wedges fill a half-turn.

tools.name: Equal wedges
tools.why: The ends are horizontal, so the arch spans $180^\circ$.

tools.name: Isosceles triangle
tools.why: Extending the legs makes an isosceles triangle.

tools.name: Co-interior angles
tools.why: The trapezoid's angles on a leg add to $180^\circ$.

2009B24.approach: Each trapezoid is an isosceles triangle with apex $20^\circ$ minus a smaller similar triangle. Its smaller angles are $80^\circ$, so the larger ones are $100^\circ$.

steps.title: Larger angle
steps.explain: Base angles $\tfrac{160^\circ}{2}=80^\circ$; the larger trapezoid angle is $180^\circ-80^\circ=100^\circ$.

check.q: If the smaller angle of an isosceles trapezoid is $80^\circ$, what is the larger?
check.why: Angles along a leg are supplementary.

2009B24.bridge: Get the wedge angle, then the triangle's base angles, then the supplement.
solution: Legs extended meet at the centre; $9$ wedges make $180^\circ$, so each is $20^\circ$.
The isosceles triangle has base angles $80^\circ$.
2009B24.recognize: Rings or arches of congruent wedges: the legs meet at a centre and the wedge angles add to the total turn.

2009B25.goal: Each face of a cube gets a stripe joining midpoints of one of its two pairs of opposite edges, chosen randomly. We want the probability some stripe loop goes all the way round the cube. A loop must run around one of the $3$ axes through $4$ faces.

tools.name: Ring around an axis
tools.why: Each of those faces must pick the one orientation that continues the loop.

tools.name: Disjoint events
tools.why: Two different rings would share a face needing two orientations.

2009B25.approach: For each axis, a loop needs the $4$ faces around it oriented the right way: $\tfrac1{16}$. The top and bottom are free. Rings for two axes can't happen together, so add: $3\cdot\tfrac1{16}$.

steps.title: One axis
steps.explain: The loop around the vertical axis uses the $4$ side faces, each needing a horizontal stripe: $\left(\tfrac12\right)^4$.

steps.title: Three axes
steps.explain: Any two rings share $2$ faces that would need perpendicular stripes, so the events are disjoint. Total $\tfrac3{16}$.

check.q: Can loops around two different axes both appear?
check.why: A shared face can't have both stripe directions.

2009B25.bridge: One ring has probability $\tfrac1{16}$; three disjoint choices.
solution: A ring around a given axis needs $4$ faces aligned: $\tfrac1{16}$.
The three ring events are mutually exclusive.
2009B25.shortcut: Count: $3$ axes $\times\ 2^2$ free top/bottom choices $=12$ of $2^6=64$ patterns: $\tfrac{12}{64}=\tfrac3{16}$.
2009B25.recognize: Loops on a cube: a loop around an axis uses exactly the $4$ faces around it.
